blocks.text: Most of the pancreas is exocrine and secretes pancreatic juice into the pancreatic duct, but patches of special cells, the islets of Langerhans, are endocrine. Each islet has beta cells, the more numerous, which secrete insulin, and alpha cells, which secrete glucagon.

blocks.caption: Insulin and glucagon
rows: lowers blood glucose: more uptake by cells (skeletal muscle, fat), glycogenesis in the liver, more glucose used in respiration, excess turned to fat, gluconeogenesis inhibited
raises blood glucose: mainly breaks down stored glycogen in the liver, releasing glucose into the blood

blocks.alt: Left: an oval islet of Langerhans surrounded by round exocrine acini; inside the islet many blue beta cells (insulin) and fewer red alpha cells (glucagon). Right: a cap-shaped adrenal gland on top of a dashed kidney, with a yellow outer cortex (cortisol, aldosterone) and a pink inner medulla (epinephrine, norepinephrine); a note says the medulla is controlled by nerves and the cortex by ACTH.
blocks.caption: Islets of Langerhans surrounded by exocrine portions (original diagram after Figure 16.4).
blocks.long_description: Most of the pancreas is exocrine and makes pancreatic juice, but its islets of Langerhans are endocrine: the more numerous beta cells secrete insulin, which lowers blood glucose, and the alpha cells secrete glucagon, which raises it. Each adrenal gland has an outer cortex, which makes corticosteroids such as cortisol (glucose homeostasis) and aldosterone (salt and water balance) under the control of ACTH, and an inner medulla, which makes epinephrine and norepinephrine for the fight-or-flight response under nervous control.

items: Too little insulin: diabetes mellitus (hyperglycaemia). Cells cannot take glucose from the blood, so blood glucose stays high; the excess glucose inhibits water reabsorption by the kidneys, so much urine is produced, causing dehydration and kidney damage.
Too much insulin: hypoglycaemia, below-normal blood glucose, with lethargy, dizziness, nervousness and, in extreme cases, unconsciousness.

blocks.title: Type I and type II diabetes
blocks.text: Type I (insulin-dependent) diabetes: the patient lacks insulin-secreting beta cells and is treated with daily insulin injections; insulin is a peptide and would be digested if swallowed. Injectable insulin is made by genetically engineered bacteria. Type II (non-insulin-dependent) diabetes: blood insulin is normal but the cells are less sensitive to it; the book says these patients do not need insulin and control the disease with other medicines, diet and exercise.

blocks.title: Note on the text
blocks.text: The book says type II patients 'do not require insulin'. Many are managed without it, but some people with type II diabetes do need insulin as the disease progresses.

blocks.prompt: Why does uncontrolled diabetes mellitus make a person pass a lot of urine?
blocks.explanation: The high blood glucose inhibits water reabsorption in the kidneys, so more water stays in the urine; the person becomes dehydrated.

items: Islets: beta cells (insulin, lowers glucose), alpha cells (glucagon, raises it).
Too little insulin: diabetes mellitus (type I: no beta cells, injections; type II: insensitive cells); too much: hypoglycaemia.
